theme: Make a joyful noise; God tested us
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 66:1-12. You read the opening verses of this psalm in Unit 3. Today you read further, to the part where the psalmist remembers the times God tested his people. Notice how the praise turns from the whole earth to the experience of Israel, and how God’s discipline is described as both fire and a spacious place.
settingTheScene: This week begins with a psalm of praise that moves from the global to the personal. The psalmist first calls the whole earth to shout to God, and then recalls the exodus and the crossing of the sea, and finally speaks about the nation’s hard experiences. It fits the story of Joshua well. Israel has crossed the Jordan and stands on the edge of a conquest that will test them. The psalm reminds us that God’s tests are not meant to destroy but to refine, and that they lead to a place of abundance. It is a good psalm to read as you prepare for the walls of Jericho.
observation: The psalm opens, “Shout for joy to God, all the earth” (v. 1), and calls people to sing the glory of his name.
“Say to God, How awesome are your deeds!” (v. 3). Even enemies cringe before his power.
“He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot” (v. 6). Both crossings are recalled.
“He rules by his might forever, his eyes keep watch on the nations” (v. 7).
God “has kept us among the living and has not let our feet slip” (v. 9).
“For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried” (v. 10).
The imagery of hardship is vivid: nets, burdens on the back, men riding over heads, fire and water (vv. 11-12).
The psalm ends this section with “yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance” (v. 12).
interpretation:
Psalm 66 reminds us that praise and hardship belong together. The psalmist does not say that life has been easy. He says that God has tested his people the way a refiner tests silver, and that the testing was real. Israel went into the net. They felt a heavy weight on their backs. They felt men trample them, and they walked through fire and flood. The psalm does not shrink from describing the pain. And yet it begins with a shout of joy.

What allows the psalmist to praise God in the middle of hardship? The answer is in the sequence. Verses 5-7 remind the people of the God who turned the sea into dry land. Verse 8 says he “has kept us among the living.” The pain was real, but so was God’s presence in it. Every hardship has a boundary that God has set. The fire and water do not overwhelm. They are the way to a place of abundance.

The word “tested” is important. In the Bible, God does not test people to find out something he does not know. He tests to reveal and to refine. A silversmith heats the metal to burn off the dross and leave pure silver. In the same way, God allows pressure so that what is false in our faith will fall away and what is true will remain. This is the same logic you will see in Joshua. The conquest is not only a military campaign but a test of whether Israel will trust God’s word and keep his covenant. Some of the hardest tests will come after the greatest victories.

The final phrase, “a place of abundance,” lifts the eyes. Hardship is not the end of the story. It is a corridor. The God who brings his people through fire and water brings them out into a spacious place. For the Christian, this finds its fullest sense in Christ, who passed through the waters of death, the “fire” of God’s judgment, and rose to the abundance of new life. His people follow him through the same journey, and the end is not loss but fullness.
connection: The first seven verses recall the exodus (Exodus 14-15) and the Jordan crossing (Joshua 3). The image of refining silver appears in Proverbs 17:3, Zechariah 13:9, and 1 Peter 1:6-7. Isaiah 43:2 promises that God will be with his people through water and fire. The “place of abundance” anticipates the land of promise and the new creation in Revelation 21.
application:
When you face hardship, avoid the two easy conclusions that God has abandoned you or that you have failed some test. Instead, ask what he might be refining. Take ten minutes today to name one area where you have felt pressure, and pray: “Lord, what do you want to burn away, and what do you want to keep?”

Also, practice praising God before the pressure lifts. The psalmist begins with a shout. Choose one song or psalm and sing or read it aloud today, even if your circumstances have not changed.

Finally, remind yourself of the place of abundance. Hardship in Christ is never wasted.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for testing you and keeping you among the living.
Tell him what pressure you are under and trust him in it.
Ask him to burn away what does not belong in you.
